nameStory: Wood stitchwort gets its name from both its preferred shady forest habitat and an old folk belief about its healing powers. The "stitchwort" part comes from medieval times when people thought this plant could heal internal "stitches" or sharp pains in the side, making it a go-to remedy for what we'd now call muscle cramps.
description: Wood stitchwort is a low-growing perennial wildflower that spreads by underground runners called stolons. It produces delicate white star-shaped flowers and has soft, oval leaves that feel slightly succulent to the touch. This woodland plant typically grows 6-12 inches tall and forms loose, spreading patches in shaded areas where few other flowers dare to bloom.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers with 5 deeply notched petals that look almost like 10 narrow petals arranged in a perfect star shape, blooming from late spring into summer

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Soft, oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, with a slightly fleshy texture that feels cool and smooth when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading colonies through underground runners, creating loose patches of plants that seem to appear randomly across the forest floor

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Weak, somewhat sprawling stems that may lean on other plants for support, often with a slightly reddish tinge at the joints where leaves attach

habitat: Wood stitchwort thrives in moist, shaded woodland areas with rich, organic soil. Look for it along stream banks, in deciduous or mixed forests, and in areas where the soil stays consistently damp but not waterlogged.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early, with fresh green shoots appearing as soil warms. Late spring brings the first delicate white flowers.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant star-shaped flowers continuing through mid-summer. Foliage remains lush and green in shaded spots.
seasonality.fall: Flowering winds down and leaves may take on yellowish tones. Seeds are dispersed and plants begin preparing for dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, surviving underground via its spreading root system and waiting for spring's return.

funFact: Despite having only one recorded observation in all of New England, wood stitchwort is actually quite common across northern Europe and Asia, making any New England sighting a genuine botanical treasure hunt discovery!
confusionNotes: Wood stitchwort is most easily confused with common chickweed, but wood stitchwort has much more deeply notched petals that create a distinctive 10-pointed star effect, while common chickweed's petals are only shallowly notched. Remember: wood stitchwort makes perfect stars, chickweed makes messy ones.
contextualKnowledge: The entire stitchwort and chickweed group can be confusing because many species look remarkably similar and their common names are often used interchangeably in different regions. What makes identification even trickier is that most field guides focus on the more common species, leaving rare ones like wood stitchwort poorly documented.
compareHints: Wood stitchwort differs from its chickweed cousins mainly in its deeper petal notches and preference for consistently moist woodland soils. While common chickweed thrives in disturbed areas and lesser stitchwort prefers grasslands, wood stitchwort is the true shade-lover of the group. Its leaves are also more oval and succulent-feeling compared to the narrower, thinner leaves of most other Stellaria species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Stellaria relatives in New England, common chickweed is the only one with that telltale single line of hairs on the stem - other chickweeds and stitchworts are either hairless or fuzzy all over.

Lesser stitchwort differs from common chickweed by having much narrower, grass-like leaves instead of oval ones, and deeply notched petals that create a clear star shape rather than chickweed's more rounded appearance.
Among the chickweeds and stitchworts in New England, water chickweed stands out for its wet habitat preferences and larger size.
Among New England's chickweeds and starworts, boreal starwort is distinguished by its four-angled stems and deeply-lobed petals that create pronounced star shapes.
Star chickweed stands out from other chickweeds by preferring woodland habitats over disturbed areas, and having much larger, more showy flowers than its weedy relatives.
Unlike the common chickweed found in gardens and lawns, bog stitchwort is strictly a wetland specialist with much narrower leaves.
Among New England's starworts and chickweeds, long-leaved starwort stands out for its exceptionally narrow, grass-like leaves and preference for consistently wet habitats.
Lesser chickweed differs from common chickweed by typically lacking flowers entirely and being much smaller in all dimensions.
